breaths.text: He stood before the gate of Tegel Prison and was free.
Yellow summer coat hanging on him like a sack, too wide in the shoulders, too short in the sleeves.
The others were still out there behind the wall, raking potatoes in rows, backs bent, guards strolling.
Franz Biberkopf stood alone.
The gate clanged shut behind him with a sound like a bank vault.
Iron.
Final.
He didn’t move.
The coat smelled of mothballs and old sweat.
His own sweat from four years back.
You think that’s it, Franz?
One step and the world is yours again?
Don’t kid yourself.
A tram came grinding along the street, number 41, bright red, sparks spitting from the overhead wire.
People inside reading newspapers, women with shopping nets, a boy with a schoolbag.
Normal people.
Franz’s legs wouldn’t carry him.
The tram stopped, doors hissed open, conductor looked at him once, twice, then rang the bell.
The 41 rolled on without Franz Biberkopf.
He stood there.
The gate was closed.
The potatoes were still being raked.
Everything behind him still moved according to rules.
Everything in front of him moved according to no rules at all.
Another 41 came.
This time he grabbed the handrail like a drowning man and swung himself up the steps.
The car was half full.
He squeezed onto the wooden bench between a fat woman in a flowered dress and a man reading the B.Z. am Mittag.
The pain hit him then, right in the middle of the chest, like someone was pulling a tooth with pliers and no cocaine.
Not a tooth in his mouth.
A tooth somewhere deeper.
The city itself, maybe.
Or what was left of him.
“Alexanderplatz next stop but three,” the conductor called.
Berlin rushed at him.
Houses, chimneys, advertisements, everything screaming.
Kaffee HAG.
Drink it and sleep like a baby.
BOSCH spark plugs.
Wrigley’s Spearmint.
The flavor lasts.
Vote List 4 Social Democrats.
Lanolin cream for soft hands.
The red-white-blue posters of the Reichsbanner.
A horse pulling a beer wagon, hooves ringing on the pavement like pistol shots.
Franz stared out the window.
The tram rattled over the tracks, swayed around curves.
Every jolt went straight into that pulled-tooth place.
He kept his fists jammed between his knees.
The fat woman beside him smelled of onions and cheap perfume.
She glanced at his yellow coat, at his prison haircut, at the way he sat like a man expecting to be hit.
“You all right, mister? ”
He didn’t answer.
Couldn’t.
The words were still locked up back in Tegel with the potatoes.
You’re out now, Franz.
Four years for manslaughter and here you are riding the 41 like any other citizen.
Congratulations.
The city doesn’t give a damn.
Look at it.
It’s already chewing up the next batch of fools.
The tram passed factories, tenements, a schoolyard where kids screamed during recess.
A Salvation Army band on a corner: trombone, drum, a girl in a poke bonnet shaking a collection box.
“Repent, the Kingdom is at hand!
” The trombone slid into a sour note.
Franz almost laughed.
Almost.
The sound died in his throat.
He saw himself from outside.
Big man in a yellow coat that didn’t fit, sitting among the living, eyes wide like a cow at the slaughterhouse gate.
The iron gates had closed.
That part was true.
But the other gates—the ones in front—those were wide open and howling.
The conductor rang again.
“Schönholzer Straße! ”
Too early.
Franz jumped up anyway.
The fat woman had to pull in her knees.
He stumbled down the steps, almost fell when the tram jerked forward again.
The door slammed.
The 41 rattled away into the traffic, sparks flying, taking its normal people with it.
Now he was standing on the pavement.
Berlin hit him full force.
Noise.
Smell of gasoline, horse piss, coal smoke, frying sausages from a stand.
People shoving past.
A cyclist nearly ran him down.
“Watch where you’re going, you idiot! ”
Franz flinched.
The voice sounded like a guard’s.
He crossed the street without looking, horns blared, a truck swerved.
He reached the other side alive.
Somehow.
He walked.
Legs moving but the rest of him still back at the prison gate.
The yellow coat flapped around his calves.
He kept his head down, eyes on the pavement cracks.
Every shop window was a threat.
Every face might know him.
Every uniform—postman, policeman, street sweeper—might be coming for him again.
“Biberkopf, Franz, born 1890, convicted of manslaughter, released today. ”
The words were written on his forehead.
He was sure of it.
He passed a newspaper kiosk. Headlines screamed:
STINNES CONCERN COLLAPSES Hugenberg demands new elections Boxer Schmeling wins again Weather: continuing warm, possible thunderstorms in the evening.
A radio in an open window played the newest hit: “Yes, we have no bananas.
” The melody hopped along like a one-legged man.
Franz stopped, listened, felt something crack inside.
Not the tooth this time.
Something smaller.
He didn’t know what.
You wanted to be decent, Franz.
You swore it on the Bible when they let you out.
“I will be decent.
” Fine words.
The city is already laughing at them.
He turned into a side street.
Fewer people.
A woman hanging laundry in a courtyard, sheets flapping like surrender flags.
Two boys kicking a ball against a wall.
Thump.
Thump.
The sound followed him.
Pain in his chest again.
Sharp, pulling.
He leaned against a lamppost.
The metal was warm from the sun.
He closed his eyes.
Behind the lids he saw the potato field, the rakes moving in steady rhythm, the guards with their rifles.
The gate closing.
The gate closing forever.
When he opened his eyes a man was standing in front of him.
Old coat, cap pulled low, face like a dried plum.
“Spare a cigarette, brother? ”
Franz shook his head.
No cigarettes.
No money.
Nothing but the yellow coat and the papers in his pocket that said he was free.
The man shrugged and moved on.
“Suit yourself, pal. ”
Franz started walking again.
Faster now.
The fear was growing.
It had teeth.
It had claws.
The city was too big, too loud, too alive.
It wanted to swallow him whole and spit out the bones.
He saw trams everywhere, all of them number 41, all of them leaving without him.
He saw his own face reflected in a butcher’s window between hanging sausages.
The face looked terrified.
Somewhere a church bell struck eleven.
The sound rolled over the rooftops like judgment.
Franz counted the strokes.
Eleven.
He had been free for exactly two hours and seventeen minutes.
He turned another corner.
Alexanderplatz was still far off but he could feel it pulling at him, a black hole sucking in people, cars, horses, trams, newspaper boys, whores, thieves, war cripples, everyone.
The center of the world.
His world now.
A scrap of paper blew against his leg.
He picked it up without thinking.
“Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord. ” —Acts 3:19
He crumpled it and threw it into the gutter.
The water carried it away between horse droppings.
You don’t need that, Franz.
You need a drink.
You need a woman.
You need to forget the potatoes and the rakes and the iron gate that closed with the sound of money in a cash register.
But the pain kept pulling.
Like a bad tooth that wouldn’t come out clean.
Like the city itself had its forceps around his heart and was yanking.
He walked on.
The yellow coat glowed in the sunlight like a warning flag.
People stared.
He didn’t care anymore.
Let them stare.
Let the whole damn city stare.
Franz Biberkopf was back.
Whether the city wanted him or not. (Word count: 1,127)
Tegel spits you out, Franz, and the gate clangs shut behind your back like a cheap tin can.
Four years inside and now the sky’s too big, the air’s got teeth.
You stand there in your thin civilian coat, shoulders hunched, the old prison smell still clinging to your neck.
Move, you idiot.
The tram rattles past on its iron rails, sparks snapping blue overhead.
Number 27.
Wedding, Müllerstraße, Alex.
But you’re not ready for Alex.
Not yet.
Your feet start anyway.
Left, right, left.
The road widens.
Factories, low barracks, a scrapyard where crows fight over something shiny.
A billboard screams: PERSIL STAYS WHITE – PERSIL WASHES WHITER.
Another one, half torn: DRINK KULMBACh.
DRINK LIFE.
The wind comes cold from the north, smells of coal and wet pine from the old Tegel woods you’re leaving behind.
You flinch at every horn.
A truck backfires – Jesus, you duck like they’re shooting at you again.
Heart banging against your ribs.
Four years of quiet and now the whole world’s yelling.
You want to turn around.
Just walk back, bang on the gate, tell them you changed your mind.
Inside was warm.
Inside had rules.
Inside you knew when they’d hit you and when they’d leave you alone.
Out here everything’s loose, flapping, dangerous.
A fat woman with a shopping net full of cabbages bumps your elbow.
“Watch it, soldier!
” she barks.
You almost apologize.
Almost say yes ma’am like you’re still wearing stripes.
Shop windows slide by.
A butcher’s: blood-red sausages hanging like fat fingers, a sign in old German script: FRESH LIVERWURST – BEST IN TEGEL.
Next door a pharmacy, green cross glowing even in daylight.
VITAMINS FOR THE NERVES.
BROMIDE FOR SLEEP.
You stare at the glass.
Your own face looks back, pale, strange, the scar on your lip still white.
Who the hell is that?
Not the Franz Biberkopf who went in.
Not the one who’s coming out.
Just some guy standing there with his hands in his pockets like he forgot what pockets are for.
Further on.
The street gets busier.
A horse-drawn cart loaded with coal blocks the tram tracks.
Driver swearing in pure Wedding dialect, whip cracking.
“Move your Jewish ass, Moses!
” The man in front of the horse is small, black caftan flapping around his ankles, beard blowing sideways in the wind.
He’s trying to lead the horse around the obstruction.
The horse doesn’t want to know.
You stop.
Something about the little man pulls at you.
He’s talking to the horse now, soft Yiddish singsong mixed with Berlin street German.
“Nu, come on, little father, don’t make me look like a fool in front of the goyim.
One foot, that’s all I ask.
One foot. ”
The horse snorts.
The driver laughs like a drain.
You step closer without meaning to.
The little Jew notices you.
Dark eyes behind steel glasses.
He sizes you up fast – the prison pallor, the cheap suit, the way you’re standing like the sidewalk might bite.
“Friend,” he says, “you look like a man who just crawled out of a hole.
Am I right? ”
You don’t answer.
Your tongue feels thick.
He shrugs, turns back to the horse, pulls gently on the bridle.
The animal finally moves.
The cart lurches.
The driver cracks his whip again, this time in celebration.
“That’s how you talk to animals, Jew-boy! ”
The little man in the caftan comes over to you.
He’s shorter than you thought.
Smells of cinnamon and old books.
“They think yelling makes them men,” he says quietly.
“But the horse knows better.
The horse always knows. ”
You swallow.
“I was inside.
Four years. ”
He nods like you just told him the time.
“Tegel? ”
“Yeah. ”
“Welcome back to the madhouse.
” He smiles, but it’s not mean.
“First day? ”
You nod.
The tram clangs again behind you.
People streaming past – workers with lunch pails, girls in cheap coats laughing too loud, an old woman selling newspapers: B.Z.
AM MITTAG!
EXTRA!
STOCK MARKET TUMBLES!
A boy on a bicycle nearly runs you down.
“Out the way, grandpa! ”
The Jew watches you flinch.
“It’s loud, eh?
After the quiet.
Like God turned the volume all the way up. ”
You laugh once, a short bark that hurts your throat.
“I want to go back in.
Stupid, right? ”
“Not stupid.
Human.
The prison is small.
The world is big.
Big is harder.
” He reaches into his caftan, pulls out a little paper bag.
“Have a prune.
Prunes are good for the bowels and the soul. ”
You take one.
It’s sweet and sticky.
The sugar hits your blood like a memory of something decent.
Around you the street keeps shouting its montage: a radio in an open window playing “Yes, we have no bananas,” a butcher shouting “Half a pound of mince, love?
” to a customer, two cops walking past with their hands behind their backs, eyes sliding over you like you’re already trouble.
One of them mutters, “Another one fresh from the pen.
Watch that one, Karl. ”
The little man sees it too.
“They smell it on you.
Like dogs.
But you’re not a dog, are you? ”
“I don’t know what I am anymore. ”
“That’s normal.
First you were a son, then a soldier, then a criminal, then a number.
Now you’re nothing.
Nothing is the best place to start from.
From nothing God made the world, they say. ”
You look at him.
The caftan is worn at the hem.
His shoes are cracked.
But he stands there like he owns the sidewalk.
“You from around here? ”
“From everywhere.
From Poland.
From Galicia.
From the Holy Book.
From this street right now.
” He laughs softly.
“My name is Nachum.
Sometimes they call me the wandering Jew, but I sell textiles.
Same difference. ”
A gust of wind blows a newspaper against your leg.
You look down.
Headline: REPARATIONS TALKS COLLAPSE IN GENEVA.
Another line below: WEATHER – CLOUDY WITH CHANCE OF REDEMPTION.
No, that last part you made up.
Your head’s doing funny things.
Nachum sees you staring at the paper.
“They print lies and we buy them anyway.
Like life.
We know it’s a lie but we keep reading. ”
You feel the panic rising again.
The noise is too much.
The people.
The trams.
The advertisements crawling across every wall like lice: BUY ON CREDIT – PAY LATER.
VISIT THE LUNAPARK – SEE THE WORLD’S FATTEST WOMAN.
A Salvation Army band starts up on the corner, brass and drums, singing “Onward Christian Soldiers” like they want to march straight over you.
“I can’t,” you mutter.
“It’s too loud.
I’m not there yet.
Not in Berlin.
Not anywhere. ”
Nachum puts a small hand on your sleeve.
The touch is surprising.
Warm.
“Nobody’s in Berlin, Franz.
Berlin’s a verb.
It’s happening all the time and you’re just trying to catch up.
Walk with me a little.
I’m going toward Reinickendorf.
Not the real city yet.
Just the edge.
The edge is good for beginners. ”
You walk.
Your legs feel borrowed.
The caftan flaps beside you like a black flag.
He talks the whole time, jumping from German to Yiddish to bits of Bible without warning.
“‘And the Lord said unto Moses, stretch out thine hand.’ But Moses was scared too.
First time out of the palace, suddenly he’s in the desert with nothing but a stick.
You think you’re the only one who ever wanted to crawl back into a hole?
Even the prophets were yellow. ”
A tram screeches to a halt.
Sparks again.
Inside, faces pressed to the windows like pale moons.
One kid sticks his tongue out at you.
You almost smile.
Nachum keeps going.
“Look at the windows.
All the pretty things they want you to buy so you forget you’re going to die.
Ties.
Radios.
Shoes that promise to make you run faster than your own life.
It’s a game.
You don’t have to play it today.
Today you just walk. ”
You pass a bar.
Through the steamed glass you see men drinking early, laughing, slapping cards on the table.
A woman in a red hat leans against the counter, smoking.
For a second your old hunger wakes up.
Then it sinks again.
Too much.
Everything’s too much.
“I killed a man,” you say suddenly.
The words fall out like stones.
Nachum doesn’t miss a step.
“I know.
The papers said.
Ida.
With a milk jug.
Terrible.
But you paid four years.
The Holy One, blessed be He, keeps different books.
Maybe He’s still adding up the columns.
Maybe He’s waiting to see what you do now. ”
A church bell starts ringing somewhere.
Wrong hour.
Or maybe time really is broken.
You pass a construction site.
Men in overalls pouring concrete, shouting jokes about the boss’s wife.
A radio on a windowsill crackles: “This is the Funk-Stunde Berlin.
The time is eleven forty-three.
Temperature forty-one degrees Fahrenheit.
And now a foxtrot for all you lovers... ”
You stop dead.
The music claws at your chest.
Nachum waits beside you, patient as the horse had been.
“I don’t know how to be out here,” you say.
“Good.
That means you’re honest.
Liars always know exactly how to be.
Liars become salesmen.
You – you’re still raw.
Like meat.
The world will chew you, Franz.
But maybe you chew back a little. ”
He offers another prune.
You take it.
The sugar helps.
The street narrows again.
Fewer trams.
More trees.
You’re still not in the real Berlin.
Not at Alexanderplatz with its roaring trains and whores and newspaper sellers screaming the headlines into your face.
Not yet.
This is the borderland.
Factories and prayer houses and little Jewish tailors and ex-cons who don’t know which way is up.
Nachum stops at a corner.
A small synagogue hides behind a shoe shop.
The Star of David looks freshly painted.
“This is where I turn.
You keep going straight.
Or turn back.
Or stand here until the sky falls.
All choices are good choices today.
Just don’t pretend you’re the same man who went into Tegel.
That man is dead.
Good riddance. ”
He adjusts his caftan, pulls his hat lower against the wind.
“If you want to find me again, ask for Nachum the rag dealer in the Grenadierstraße.
I’ll be there.
Or I won’t.
God’s a joker. ”
You watch him walk away.
Small black figure against the gray morning.

The wind takes his words and scatters them like the newspaper pages flapping in the gutter: fragments of Psalms, stock prices, weather reports, dirty jokes, tram schedules, the distant thunder of the real city waiting up ahead.
You stand there a long time.
Still not there.
The first fat drops of rain hit your face.
You turn your collar up.
Left foot.
Right foot.
The road keeps going.
Somewhere up ahead the Alex is sharpening its knives.
But not yet.
Not yet.
**Zannowich**
Rain slants across Alexanderplatz like it’s got a grudge.
The trams clang past, sparks snapping off the wires, and the wet pavement throws back neon from the movie house: *Metropolis* still playing, robot girl kicking her chrome legs.
Franz Biberkopf stands under the awning of the Aschinger’s, sausage steam curling round his ears, collar turned up, one hand in his pocket worrying a pfennig that won’t buy him nothing.
You think you’re done with the world, Franz?
The world ain’t done with you.
A little man in a threadbare coat, collar shiny with grease, sidles up.
Smells of schnapps and yesterday’s newsprint.
“Biberkopf,” he says, like they’re old pals from Tegel.
“You look like a man what’s been buried and dug up twice.
Come on, I’ll stand you a beer.
Name’s Willy, used to push papers on the Oranienburger. ”
Franz don’t answer right away.
His head’s still full of Reinhold’s voice and the axe and the blood on the floorboards.
But the rain’s cold and the beer’s warm, so he lets himself be steered inside.
The place is loud with wet coats and wet mouths.
They sit at a marble table sticky with rings.
Two mugs arrive, foam sliding down the glass like cheap lace.
Willy leans in, eyes bright as a rat’s.
“You gotta hear this one, Franz.
Real story.
About a fella name of Zannowich.
Prince Zannowich, they called him.
Only he weren’t no prince.
Born in a stinking village in Montenegro or some such, dirt under his nails, lice in his hair.
But the boy had style.
Knew how to wear a coat even when he stole it. ”
Franz stares into the foam.
The bubbles pop slow, like they got all the time in the world. *And the Lord said unto Cain*—shut up, brain.
He drinks.
The beer tastes of iron and yesterday.
“Listen,” Willy says, tapping the table so the rings dance.
“Zannowich walks into Venice one day, nineteen years old, ragged as a beggar.
Next thing you know he’s wearing velvet, got a sword with a silver hilt, calling himself Prince of Montenegro.
People believe him.
Why?
Because he believes it harder.
He throws balls, he gambles, he fucks countesses, he borrows money from every duke and banker stupid enough to open his purse.
Lives like a comet, Franz.
Burns bright, burns fast. ”
A newspaper seller outside bawls the headlines: *STRESEMANN IN GENEVA—PEACE OR PAPER?* The tram bell clangs again.
Number 4 to Weissensee.
Franz sees a woman’s red hat flash past the window, gone.
Willy’s voice drops, confidential.
“They caught him eventually, of course.
Debt, forgery, the usual.
Threw him in the clink at Venice.
But even there—listen to this—even there the man don’t break.
He writes letters.
Beautiful letters.
Signs ’em Prince Zannowich, Imperial Highness.
The guards start calling him Your Grace.
The governor comes to visit.
They play cards.
The governor loses money and laughs about it.
That’s power, Franz.
That’s what a man can do if he decides who the hell he is. ”
Franz feels the words crawling over him like lice.
He wants to brush them off.
He wants another beer.
He wants to be left alone in the dark where nobody expects nothing.
But Willy’s leaning closer, breath like old cheese.
“Point is, Biberkopf, a man can rise.
You hear me?
From the gutter to the palace.
From the shit-heap to the silk sheets.
All it takes is deciding.
You been lying there like a dead dog since that business with Mieze.
I know.
Whole neighborhood knows.
But the dog can get up.
The dog can put on a coat and be somebody else.
Zannowich did it.
Why not you? ”
Franz’s mouth moves before his brain catches up.
“I killed her. ”
The words fall between them like a dead bird.
Willy don’t even blink.
“Everybody kills something.
Zannowich probably killed a few.
That ain’t the point.
The point is what you do after.
You can crawl back into the bottle or you can stand up and say: From now on I’m Prince Biberkopf.
I walk like a prince.
I talk like a prince.
People start believing it, and then it’s true.
That’s how the world works, Franz.
All the rest is newspaper. ”
A gust of wind slams the door open.
Rain blows in, mixed with the smell of wet horses and coal smoke.
Somebody laughs too loud at the next table. *Buy your winter coat now—only 29 marks at Wertheim’s—guaranteed pure wool.* The ad swims in Franz’s head like a fish.
He sees it for a second, the whole stupid beautiful lie: himself in a good coat, hat tilted, walking down the Friedrichstrasse like he owns the pavement.
Girls looking.
Men stepping aside.
No more hauling furniture, no more pimping, no more waking up with the shakes and the dead girl behind his eyes.
Just Prince Franz.
His Majesty the Butcher’s Son.
The vision makes him sick and hungry at the same time.
Willy’s still talking, voice rising and falling like a bad sermon.
“—and when they finally dragged him out to hang him, he wore his velvet coat to the scaffold.
Bowed to the crowd.
Said, ‘Gentlemen, I have lived as a prince and I shall die as a prince.’ They cheered him, Franz.
They actually cheered the bastard while they put the rope round his neck. ”
Franz drains the mug.
The beer’s gone flat.
His hands are shaking again.
He remembers the feel of the axe handle, the soft sound Mieze made when it hit.
Remembers Reinhold laughing.
Remembers the darkness after.
“I ain’t no prince,” he mutters.
Willy slaps the table.
“That’s exactly what you were before they broke you.
You were Franz Biberkopf, the man who don’t take shit, who walks straight, who says what he means.
They knocked you down.
So get up different.
Get up better.
Be Zannowich.
Be anything but this.
” He waves a hand at Franz like he’s a pile of rags.
The jukebox in the corner starts up—scratchy record, some girl singing about a blue heaven.
Outside the rain’s turning to sleet.
The neon flickers. *Kaffee HAG—caffeine-free—good for the nerves.*
Franz feels something move in his chest, something small and mean and alive.
He hates it.
He wants it.
He wants to stay dead and he wants to live so bad it hurts his teeth.
Willy stands up, throws coins on the table.
“Think about it, Prince.
The city’s full of coats waiting to be worn.
Full of names waiting to be taken.
Don’t let ’em bury you twice. ”
He tips his greasy hat and slips out into the weather.
The door swings shut.
Franz sits there alone with the empty mugs and the wet rings and the voice in his head that won’t shut up.
*And the Lord said, What hast thou done?
The voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.*
Franz closes his eyes.
Sees velvet.
Sees a rope.
Sees himself walking down Unter den Linden in a coat that costs more than a year’s rent, tipping his hat to the girls, smiling like a man who never swung an axe in his life.
The tram clangs past again.
Number 9 this time.
Sparks.
Rain.
The city keeps moving whether you’re dead or alive.
You gonna stay under that awning forever, Franz?
Or you gonna put the coat on?
He stands up slow.
Legs like wood.
Pays for the beers with the last of his money.
Steps out into the sleet.
The wind hits him full in the face, cold as judgment.
He pulls his collar higher.
For a second he straightens his back the way the little man said.
Tries the walk.
Just a little.
Chin up.
Eyes forward.
A girl hurries past under an umbrella, gives him a quick look.
Not afraid.
Not pitying.
Just a look.
Franz Biberkopf—maybe Prince Zannowich for a minute—keeps walking.
The sleet stings his eyes.
His heart’s hammering like it wants to break out and run ahead of him.

A different man.

Didn’t.

The not-doing.

He’s seen whiter.

Second person now, because you, Franz, you think you’re smarter this time.
You think the city won’t grab you by the neck again.

Good boy.

One, two, three street corners without looking back.

” Franz keeps walking.
The city does not own him the same way.
Not today.

“Idiot!

This has smell.

No reaching.
Not yet.

The night watchman inside him nods approval.
Dear fatherland, be calm.
He has his eyes open.

One foot.
